claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can initially exist as a single-phase solid solution.
Their elevated-temperature structural evolution is governed by competition between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-energy-driven phase segregation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution phase.
Surface-energy minimization drives phase segregation in these nanoparticles.
Below a critical nanoparticle size, surface-energy effects dominate configurational-entropy stabilization.
Heating above 0.5 Tm under an inert atmosphere can reveal the proposed thermally driven structural evolution.
Surface-to-volume ratio and interfacial-energy gradients mediate nanoparticle structural evolution.
At the nanoscale, surface-energy minimization contributes more strongly to lowering total Gibbs free energy than the configurational-entropy term, TΔS_conf.
Heating allows the nanoparticles to overcome kinetic barriers to phase separation.
Phase separation produces elemental or binary-rich domains.
Nanoparticles smaller than a critical size, provisionally suggested as below 5 nm, will segregate or form core-shell structures upon heating.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk counterparts will remain single-phase under comparable heating.
Traditional high-entropy-alloy theory predicts intrinsic solid-solution stability from high configurational entropy regardless of particle size when bulk thermodynamics is assumed to dominate.
The proposed mechanism ceases to apply in bulk materials or in particles larger than the critical size because configurational entropy then dominates surface-energy effects.
Retention of a single-phase solid solution across the full 2–50 nm size range after annealing at 0.6 Tm for one hour would falsify the proposed small-particle segregation hypothesis.
